title: Democracy: Deliberation, Epistocracy and Its Discontents
subtitle: Should the people rule, should they talk first, or should the knowledgeable rule instead?
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish aggregative, deliberative and epistemic conceptions of democracy
By the end you will be able to work through the Condorcet jury theorem with numbers and state its assumptions
By the end you will be able to explain Habermas's deliberative democracy and Rawls's idea of public reason
By the end you will be able to present Brennan's case for epistocracy and the strongest democratic replies
hook:
Suppose you need surgery. Would you want the procedure chosen by a vote of everyone in the hospital waiting room? Of course not. You want an expert. So why do we let everyone, including people who cannot name their own representatives, vote on war, taxes and climate policy?

Plato asked exactly this (Day 14), comparing democracy to a ship where the crew, ignorant of navigation, fights over the wheel. For most of history his answer, that the wise should rule, seemed obvious to the educated. Today most of us find it offensive. But offence is not an argument. This lesson examines three modern ways of defending democracy: as a way of adding up preferences, as a process of public reasoning, and as a surprisingly smart way of finding the truth. Then it faces the most serious modern challenger, the proposal called **epistocracy**: rule by the knowledgeable.

sections.heading: Three Ways to Think About Democracy
sections.body:
Ask what democracy is *for*, and you get at least three answers.

On the **aggregative** view, democracy is a fair procedure for combining people's preferences. Everyone has interests; voting adds them up; the majority wins. Democracy's value lies in **political equality**: each person counts for one. This view does not care whether the outcome is wise, only that it fairly reflects what people want.

The **deliberative** view says that is too thin. Preferences are not fixed; they can be informed, challenged and changed. Democracy at its best is a process in which citizens exchange reasons and justify their positions to one another before deciding. Its legitimacy comes from the quality of that public reasoning, not just from counting.

The **epistemic** view says democracy is valuable partly because it tends to get the *right answers*: to identify policies that actually serve the common good. On this view a democratic decision is like a jury verdict: there is a fact of the matter, and the procedure is good at tracking it.

These views can combine. But they come apart in hard cases. An aggregative democrat has no complaint if voters choose a ruinous policy fairly. An epistemic democrat does, and must face an awkward question: if what matters is getting things right, why not let those most likely to be right make the decisions? That is the opening the epistocrats exploit.

sections.heading: Condorcet's Jury Theorem: A Worked Example
sections.body:
The **Marquis de Condorcet** (1743–1794) was a mathematician and Enlightenment reformer who died in prison during the French Revolution. In 1785 he proved a result now called the **Condorcet jury theorem**. It is the mathematical heart of epistemic democracy.

Suppose a group faces a yes-or-no question with a correct answer. Assume:

1. Each voter is more likely to be right than wrong (call the probability p, with p greater than 0.5).
2. Voters judge **independently** of one another.
3. The group decides by simple majority.

Then the probability that the majority is right is higher than any individual's, and it approaches certainty as the group grows.

Let's check with numbers. Take three voters, each right with probability 0.6. The majority is right if all three are right, or exactly two are.

- All three right: 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.216.
- Exactly two right: there are three ways this can happen (voter A wrong, or B, or C), each with probability 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.144. So 3 × 0.144 = 0.432.
- Total: 0.216 + 0.432 = 0.648.

So three modestly competent voters (60%) make a group that is right 64.8% of the time. With 101 such voters, the majority is right about 98% of the time; with thousands, it is practically certain.

Now the sting. Run the same calculation with p = 0.4. All three right: 0.064. Exactly two: 3 × (0.4 × 0.4 × 0.6) = 0.288. Total: 0.352. The group is *worse* than an individual, and with a large electorate it is almost certain to be wrong. Majority rule amplifies whatever competence or incompetence exists.

And the independence assumption matters too. If voters all copy one pundit or one news feed, a million votes are worth little more than one. The theorem therefore tells us what democracy needs to work well: voters who are better than chance on the question at hand and who think somewhat independently.

sections.heading: Habermas and Deliberative Democracy
sections.body:
The leading theorist of deliberation is the German philosopher **Jürgen Habermas** (born 1929), heir to the Frankfurt School you met on Day 80. Habermas grew up in Nazi Germany, and his work can be read as a lifelong search for what makes a free public sphere possible.

His central idea is **communicative rationality**. Much human action is *strategic*: we try to get others to do what we want, by bribery, threat or manipulation. But when we argue sincerely, we implicitly accept certain norms: that we are telling the truth, that we will accept good reasons, that anyone affected may speak. Habermas famously describes the ideal as one where nothing compels agreement except the force of the better argument.

From this he derives a **discourse principle**: the only norms that are valid are those that all affected persons could agree to as participants in rational discourse. Democracy, in his *Between Facts and Norms* (1992), is the institutional attempt to approximate this. Legitimacy flows from a healthy **public sphere**, the network of newspapers, associations, cafés and (today) online forums where citizens form opinions, feeding into parliaments that turn those opinions into law.

Critics raise sharp objections. Iris Marion Young argued that idealised 'rational argument' often favours the educated, articulate and calm, and excludes styles of speech, like testimony or protest, used by marginalised groups. Others note that deliberation can make groups *more* extreme: Cass Sunstein's research on **group polarisation** found that like-minded people who discuss an issue often end up with more extreme versions of their original view. Deliberation is not magic; its design matters.

sections.heading: Public Reason: What Counts as a Reason in Politics?
sections.body:
A close cousin of deliberative democracy is Rawls's idea of **public reason**, developed in *Political Liberalism* (1993) and his essay *The Idea of Public Reason Revisited* (1997). You saw last lesson that Rawls takes **reasonable pluralism** as a permanent fact: citizens hold different religions and philosophies.

If so, what reasons may I offer when I support a law that will be enforced on everyone? Rawls's **liberal principle of legitimacy** says political power is legitimate only when exercised in accordance with a constitution whose essentials all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse. In practice this means that, on fundamental questions, citizens and officials should justify their positions with reasons others can accept as free and equal people: appeals to liberty, equality, fairness, public health, rather than to doctrines only some share, like a particular reading of scripture.

Consider a worked example. A legislator wants to restrict gambling. If her argument is 'gambling is a sin according to my faith', that is not a public reason, since non-believers cannot be expected to accept it. If her argument is 'gambling machines cause measurable addiction and family breakdown', that is a public reason, open to evidence anyone can assess. Rawls added a **proviso**: religious reasons may be introduced in public debate, provided that in due course proper public reasons are also given.

Critics ask whether this is fair to religious citizens. Nicholas Wolterstorff argued that many believers cannot separate their political views from their faith, and that demanding they do so places an unequal burden on them. Habermas proposed a compromise: citizens may speak in religious terms in the public sphere, but laws themselves must be justified in a language accessible to all, with secular citizens sharing the work of 'translation'.

sections.heading: Brennan's Case for Epistocracy
sections.body:
In *Against Democracy* (2016), the American philosopher **Jason Brennan** launched the most prominent recent attack. He sorts citizens into three types:

- **Hobbits**: largely uninterested and uninformed about politics.
- **Hooligans**: passionate partisans who consume information selectively, like sports fans, to cheer their team.
- **Vulcans** (after Mr Spock): who reason scientifically and change their minds with the evidence.

Brennan argues that most citizens are hobbits or hooligans, citing decades of survey research showing widespread ignorance of basic political facts. Worse, political participation tends to make people *more* hooligan-like, not more thoughtful.

His central argument rests on a **competence principle**: it is unjust to deprive people of life, liberty or property, or to harm them significantly, through decisions made by incompetent or bad-faith bodies. We would reject a jury that ignored the evidence. An electorate that votes in ignorance, Brennan says, is like such a jury, and its decisions are imposed on everyone, including those who voted wisely.

Hence **epistocracy**: systems in which political power is formally distributed according to knowledge or competence. Brennan floats several designs: restricting the vote to those who pass a basic test of political knowledge; giving extra votes to the better informed (echoing John Stuart Mill's proposal of **plural voting**, which you met with Mill on Day 62); an **epistocratic council** with power to veto democratic decisions; or an **enfranchisement lottery**, where a randomly chosen group of citizens earns the vote by passing a competence-building process.

Brennan is careful to say that this is a conditional, empirical case: if some epistocracy would produce substantially better results, we should try it, perhaps first at small scale.

sections.heading: Democratic Replies
sections.body:
Defenders of democracy have several strong answers.

**The demographic objection.** Knowledge tests would not be neutral. Political knowledge correlates with income, education, race and sex, so epistocracy would give more power to already-advantaged groups, whose interests it would then serve. America's history of literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters is a grim warning. Brennan replies that a knowledgeable electorate might still vote for the public good; critics doubt it.

**Estlund's 'expert/boss fallacy'.** In *Democratic Authority* (2008), David Estlund grants that some people know more than others. But he argues it does not follow that they should rule. Being an expert does not make you a boss. For any proposed group of experts, reasonable people could object to their selection, their biases or their blind spots. Legitimate power needs a justification that every reasonable citizen could accept, what Estlund calls the **qualified acceptability requirement**, and no epistocratic selection can meet it. Democracy is not infallible, but it is the best procedure acceptable to all.

**Diversity trumps ability.** Hélène Landemore's *Democratic Reason* (2013) draws on a mathematical result by Lu Hong and Scott Page suggesting that, under certain conditions, a diverse group of problem-solvers outperforms a group of the individually best ones, because the best tend to think alike and get stuck in the same places. Large, inclusive groups bring more perspectives. This is an epistemic argument *for* inclusion, not against it.

**Political equality has intrinsic value.** Finally, many insist that being denied a vote is an expressive insult: it publicly marks you as a lesser citizen. Even if epistocracy produced slightly better policies, the cost to equal status might be too high. Perhaps the better response to voter ignorance is to improve the conditions of deliberation rather than to shrink the electorate.

modernConnection.title: Citizens' Assemblies: Democracy by Lottery
modernConnection.body:
A quiet experiment is spreading through democracies, combining insights from both sides of this debate. A **citizens' assembly** gathers a randomly selected, demographically representative group of ordinary people, gives them time, expert briefings and trained facilitators, and asks them to deliberate on a hard question.

The best-known case is Ireland. Its Citizens' Assembly (2016–2018), made up of 99 citizens chosen at random plus a chairperson, considered among other topics the constitutional ban on abortion. After weekends of testimony and discussion, members recommended reform by large margins. The government put the question to a referendum in 2018, and voters approved changing the constitution. France's Citizens' Convention on Climate (2019–2020), with 150 randomly chosen members, produced 149 proposals, though many were later watered down by the government, prompting criticism that the process had been used for show.

Look at the logic. Random selection (called **sortition**, used in ancient Athens to fill many offices) preserves political equality: everyone has the same chance of being picked, and the group mirrors the public. Structured deliberation addresses Brennan's worry about hobbits and hooligans: members become informed and are encouraged to reason, not cheer. And the diversity of the group draws on Landemore's argument. Some researchers, like James Fishkin with his **deliberative polls**, have found that participants' views often shift substantially after deliberation, and not always toward the elite consensus.

The limits are real. Assemblies are small and can be steered by whoever sets the agenda or picks the experts. Their recommendations lack democratic authority unless a parliament or referendum adopts them. Still, they suggest the choice is not simply between the uninformed many and the expert few.

vocabulary.definition: The view that democracy is valuable partly because it tends to produce correct or good decisions.
vocabulary.example: Defenders of epistemic democracy point to the Condorcet jury theorem.

vocabulary.definition: The result that if independent voters are each more likely right than wrong, a majority is more likely right than any individual, approaching certainty as the group grows.
vocabulary.example: The Condorcet jury theorem also warns that if voters are worse than chance, larger majorities are more reliably wrong.

vocabulary.definition: A view on which democratic legitimacy depends on citizens publicly exchanging and responding to reasons before deciding.
vocabulary.example: A town meeting where residents debate a new road before voting is a small exercise in deliberative democracy.

vocabulary.definition: Rawls's ideal that fundamental political decisions be justified by reasons all reasonable citizens can be expected to accept.
vocabulary.example: Appealing to public health rather than to scripture is an appeal to public reason.

vocabulary.definition: A system in which political power is formally distributed according to knowledge or competence.
vocabulary.example: Giving extra votes to people who pass a civics test would be a form of epistocracy.

vocabulary.definition: Brennan's principle that it is unjust to impose high-stakes decisions on people through incompetent or bad-faith decision-makers.
vocabulary.example: Brennan argues an ignorant electorate violates the competence principle, just as a careless jury would.

vocabulary.definition: The tendency of like-minded groups to adopt more extreme positions after discussing an issue among themselves.
vocabulary.example: A forum of only climate sceptics may become more sceptical after debate, illustrating group polarisation.

vocabulary.definition: Selecting public officials or decision-makers by random lottery.
vocabulary.example: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly used sortition to choose its members.

thinkingExercise.title: Design a Decision Procedure
thinkingExercise.prompt: Your country must decide whether to build a major nuclear power programme. Design the decision procedure you think is most legitimate, and test it against the objections from this lesson.
steps: Choose a procedure: a referendum, a parliamentary vote, a citizens' assembly, an expert commission, an epistocratic veto, or a combination.
Check it against the Condorcet jury theorem: are participants likely better than chance on this question? Do they judge independently?
Check it against public reason and the demographic objection: could every reasonable citizen accept it? Who would be over- or under-represented?
Write a short paragraph defending your design to a citizen who strongly opposes the outcome it produces. Does your defence rely on equality, good outcomes or good reasoning?

summary: Democracy can be defended as fair aggregation, as public deliberation, or as a reliable way of tracking correct answers.
The Condorcet jury theorem shows majorities amplify individual competence, for better (p above 0.5) or worse (p below 0.5), and depends on independence.
Habermas grounds legitimacy in communicative reason and a healthy public sphere; Rawls's public reason asks for justifications all reasonable citizens can accept.
Brennan argues that widespread voter ignorance violates a competence principle and favours experimenting with epistocracy.
Replies include the demographic objection, Estlund's expert/boss fallacy, diversity-trumps-ability arguments and the intrinsic value of equal status.

quiz.question: Three independent voters are each right with probability 0.6. What is the probability that the majority is right?
quiz.explanation: All three right (0.216) plus exactly two right (3 × 0.144 = 0.432) gives 0.648.

quiz.question: According to the Condorcet jury theorem, adding more voters always makes a majority more likely to be correct.
quiz.explanation: Only if each voter is better than chance and votes independently; if voters are below 0.5, more voters make the majority more reliably wrong.

quiz.question: Which scenario most clearly undermines the Condorcet jury theorem's independence assumption?
options: Most voters base their choice on a single viral video
quiz.explanation: If voters all follow the same source, their judgments are correlated, so the group adds little beyond that one source.

quiz.question: For Habermas, legitimate norms are those that:
options: All affected could agree to as participants in rational discourse
quiz.explanation: This is Habermas's discourse principle, rooted in communicative rationality.

quiz.question: Which argument for a law would satisfy Rawls's ideal of public reason?
options: My ancestors always lived this way
Evidence shows it reduces child poverty, which matters to all citizens as equals
The leader I trust supports it
quiz.explanation: Public reasons appeal to values and evidence that citizens with different worldviews can accept.

quiz.question: In Brennan's typology, a passionate partisan who seeks out only news that flatters his side is a:
quiz.explanation: Hooligans consume political information like sports fans, selectively and tribally.

quiz.question: John Stuart Mill proposed giving more votes to better-educated citizens.
quiz.explanation: Mill's plural voting proposal appears in Considerations on Representative Government (1861).

quiz.question: Estlund's 'expert/boss fallacy' is the mistake of thinking that:
options: Because someone knows more, they are entitled to rule over others
quiz.explanation: Estlund argues knowledge alone does not confer authority; the selection of experts must be acceptable to all reasonable citizens.

quiz.question: The 'demographic objection' to epistocracy claims that:
options: Knowledge tests would shift power toward already advantaged groups
Populations are too large for voting
Experts are always biased toward the poor
quiz.explanation: Measured political knowledge correlates with education, income and other advantages, so epistocracy could entrench them.

quiz.question: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly was made up of elected politicians chosen for their expertise.
quiz.explanation: Its citizen members were chosen at random to be broadly representative of the public.

goDeeper.body:
Condorcet also discovered a darker result. With three or more options, majority preferences can be **cyclic**. Suppose voter 1 ranks A over B over C, voter 2 ranks B over C over A, and voter 3 ranks C over A over B. Then a majority prefers A to B, a majority prefers B to C, and a majority prefers C to A. There is no stable 'will of the people'; whoever controls the order of votes controls the outcome. In 1951 the economist Kenneth Arrow generalised this into his **impossibility theorem**: no method of turning individual rankings into a group ranking can satisfy a small set of seemingly obvious fairness conditions at once, unless it is a dictatorship.

William Riker's *Liberalism Against Populism* (1982) used these results to argue that the populist idea of a coherent popular will is an illusion; democracy's value is only that it lets voters remove rulers. Deliberative democrats responded that discussion can create **single-peaked preferences**, a shared sense of the dimension along which options lie (say, from more to less government spending), and under single-peakedness cycles disappear. Experiments by Christian List, James Fishkin and colleagues found some evidence that deliberation does increase single-peakedness. So the debate between deliberative and social-choice theorists has become partly empirical: can good discussion rescue the idea of a collective will from Arrow's theorem?

readings.title: Against Democracy
readings.author: Jason Brennan
readings.note: Readable and provocative; chapters 1 and 8 contain the hobbit/hooligan typology and the proposals for epistocracy.

readings.title: Democratic Authority
readings.author: David Estlund
readings.note: Demanding; chapter 1 and the discussion of the expert/boss fallacy are the key parts.

readings.title: Democratic Reason
readings.author: Hélène Landemore
readings.note: A defence of the collective intelligence of the many, drawing on Condorcet and Hong and Page.

readings.title: Political Liberalism
readings.author: John Rawls
readings.note: Lecture VI sets out the idea of public reason.

questions: If an epistocracy reliably produced better outcomes for the poor, would that answer the demographic objection?
Should religious arguments be welcome in parliamentary debate, or only in the wider public sphere?
Could social media be redesigned to make citizens more like Vulcans and less like hooligans?
